diagram_name: Two Ends of the Serpent Column
learning_objective: The learner will attribute each of 10 claims about the Serpent Column to the place where its evidence can be checked, at Delphi, in Istanbul, or only in an ancient written source, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** serpent-column-two-ends
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Analyze
**Bloom Verb:** attribute
**Learning Objective:** The learner will attribute each of 10 claims about the Serpent Column to the place where its evidence can be checked, at Delphi, in Istanbul, or only in an ancient written source, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** Serpent Column, Plataea and the Persian Wars (Chapter 15), the Hippodrome (Chapter 4), the Third Sacred War (Chapter 17), Herodotus, Thucydides and Pausanias as sources, the great altar and the temple terrace, and the polygonal wall (all defined in this chapter's Part Two or in the chapters named). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner places each of the 10 claim cards into one of three bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 8 of 10 correct on the first Check. Reading a card's hint before placing it is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Everything about the column can be seen in Istanbul, because the bronze is there. (2) Delphi has nothing left of the monument. (3) Facts in a museum label must come from the object itself, when many come from ancient writers. (4) The column was always headless. **Instructional Rationale:** Attributing each claim to its evidence is an Analyze task: the learner must separate what an object shows, what a place shows, and what only a text reports. The three bins mirror the chapter's table, so the learner rebuilds the distinction instead of reading it. **Content:** Bins, shown with these labels: "Check it at Delphi"; "Check it in Istanbul"; "Only in a written source". Claim cards, shown in a shuffled order: | # | Claim card | Correct bin | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Bronze coils carry the names of the Greek cities that fought. | Check it in Istanbul | The inscribed coils stand in the Hippodrome, where Constantine moved them. | | 2 | A stone base by the great altar marks where the monument stood. | Check it at Delphi | The base never left the sanctuary. | | 3 | A bronze copy shows how the column looked in its setting. | Check it at Delphi | The copy stands near the altar, close to where the original stood. | | 4 | The upper jaw of one serpent head survives. | Check it in Istanbul | It is in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums, beside Gülhane Park. | | 5 | The column stands in a pit because the ground has risen since Byzantine times. | Check it in Istanbul | The pit is in the Hippodrome, at about the level of the Byzantine track. | | 6 | The temple terrace where the monument stood is held up by the polygonal wall. | Check it at Delphi | We can walk along the wall below the terrace. | | 7 | The Spartan commander Pausanias had his own name inscribed first, and it was erased. | Only in a written source | Thucydides tells this story; the erased verse does not survive on the bronze. | | 8 | A golden tripod once sat on top of the three heads. | Only in a written source | Herodotus and Pausanias describe the tripod; its gold was taken long ago. | | 9 | The monument was made from a tenth of the spoils of Plataea. | Only in a written source | Herodotus gives the source of the metal; the bronze itself cannot tell us. | | 10 | The Phocian leaders took the tripod's gold during the Third Sacred War. | Only in a written source | The travel writer Pausanias reports it, about five hundred years later. | **Provenance:** All claims come from this chapter's sections "The Serpent Column" and "The Polygonal Wall" and from Chapter 4 (the Hippodrome pit, the Byzantine ground level). Bin assignments follow the chapter's evidence table. **Rules:** - 10 cards and 3 bins. Each card has exactly one correct bin. - Cards are shuffled once when the sim starts; the order is the same after Reset. - A card can be moved between bins until Check is pressed. - Check is available only when all 10 cards are placed. - Score = number of cards in their correct bin, from 0 to 10. Mastery is score >= 8 on the first Check. - The correct totals are 3 for Delphi, 3 for Istanbul, and 4 for written sources. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner reads the three bin labels and the first card. 2. The learner places each card in a bin. A placed card can be moved again. 3. When all 10 cards are placed, the learner presses Check. Every card is marked correct or incorrect, and its Why text appears. 4. The learner moves the incorrect cards and presses Check again until all 10 are correct; only the first Check counts toward mastery. 5. When all cards are correct, the sim shows the three bins side by side with the summary: "Delphi has the place, Istanbul has the object, and the writers have the story." 6. The learner should notice that four of the ten claims depend on ancient writers, not on anything we can see at either end. **Feedback:** Ten cards, shuffled, unlimited re-checks. Correct card: "Correct: [why text]." Incorrect card: "Not here. [why text]" The score "Cards correct: n of 10" is shown after every Check. A Reset option clears all placements and restores the starting order. **Starting State:** Three empty bins, ten unplaced cards, and the question "The bronze is in Istanbul. What can only Delphi tell us?" **Chapter Anchors:** Plataea, 479 BCE; 31 communities named; moved by 330 CE; the Third Sacred War, 356–346 BCE; Pausanias the travel writer, 2nd century CE; the upper jaw of one head in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums; ten claims, three bins.
